## Role in the Model

This calculation turns turbine coordinates, a tabulated turbine curve and a set
of wind states into the wake-affected electrical power of every turbine in every
state. That table is the common input to all architectures: it gives power at the
generator electrical output, before any architecture-specific conversion or
collection loss. The implementation is `calculate_wakes` in
`model/wind_resource_and_layout/wake_modelling_and_spacing.py`.

The layout is deliberately schematic. It exposes the relationship between
installed capacity, occupied area, turbine separation and wake loss without
claiming to reproduce a consented or commercially optimised wind-farm layout.

## Inputs

| Symbol | Description | Unit | Source in the model |
|---|---|---:|---|
| $(x_j,y_j)$ | Turbine coordinates, $x$ east and $y$ north | m | Scenario coordinates file, or a declared regular grid |
| $P(v)$, $C_T(v)$ | Tabulated electrical power and thrust coefficient | kW, – | Scenario turbine-curve file |
| $D$, $H_h$ | Rotor diameter and hub height | m | Scenario turbine record |
| $v_s$, $\theta_s$, $h_s$ | Wind speed, direction (wind **from**, clockwise from north) and annual hours of state $s$ | m/s, °, h/year | Scenario wind-state file |
| $I_0$ | Ambient turbulence intensity | fraction | {{< var wind-turbulence-intensity >}} (provisional legacy assumption) |

The state hours must add up to the central annual-hour basis
({{< var annual-hours >}}); they are not renormalised.

## Layout

A scenario supplies coordinates directly, or declares a regular grid (turbine
count, columns, spacings and rotation) whose incomplete final row is centred.
In both cases the model checks that every pair of turbines is at least the
declared minimum separation apart and rejects the layout otherwise. Farm area is
a reporting boundary; it is never used as a multiplier on distances.

The article reference case generates its coordinates from the agreed site
record: a rectangle across the dominant wind direction, rows numbered from the
upwind edge and an explicit rotation convention (see the
[reference case](../research_articles/turbine_level_hydrogen/reference_case.qmd#sec-common-operating-case)).

## Turbine Performance

The wake calculation uses a supplied, tabulated power and thrust-coefficient
curve; it never builds a synthetic curve. The article case uses the pinned IEA
15 MW reference turbine release [@gaertner2020IEA15; @ieaWind15RwtRelease2026],
whose power column is electrical output. Zero power and thrust are declared just
outside the operating range, because PyWake would otherwise hold the first
tabulated value for waked turbines below cut-in.

## Wake Calculation

PyWake evaluates every state with the following configuration
[@pywakeDocumentation2026]:

| Model element | Selection | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Site | `UniformSite` with ambient $I_0$ | Uniform inflow; state weights come from the wind-state table, not from the site |
| Propagation | `PropagateDownwind` | Calculates wakes from upstream to downstream turbines |
| Wake deficit | `TurboNOJDeficit` | Turbulence-dependent top-hat wake expansion [@nygaard2020ClusterWakes] |
| Rotor averaging | `AreaOverlapAvgModel`, on the deficit model | Partial overlap of a top-hat wake and a downstream rotor |
| Superposition | `SquaredSum` | Combines deficits from several upstream turbines |
| Blockage | None | Upstream induction is excluded |

The calculation is run once per wind direction for all speeds in that direction;
each state keeps its own speed and weight. For state $s$ and turbine $j$ the
result is the wake-affected power $P_{j,s}$ in kW. The installed PyWake version is
recorded with each result.

## Annual Energy and Outputs

The wake-affected and no-wake annual energies, in MWh/year, are

$$
E_\mathrm{wake}=\frac{1}{1000}\sum_s h_s\sum_j P_{j,s},
\qquad
E_0=\frac{N}{1000}\sum_s h_s\,P(v_s),
$$

and the wake loss and wake-affected gross capacity factor are

$$
L_\mathrm{wake}=1-\frac{E_\mathrm{wake}}{E_0},
\qquad
CF_\mathrm{wake,gross}=\frac{1000\,E_\mathrm{wake}}{NP_r\,\sum_s h_s}.
$$

These exclude availability, collection, conversion and export losses, which are
applied downstream and must not be applied again here. For the article reference
case the result is a wake loss of {{< var ijv-wake-loss >}} and a gross capacity
factor of {{< var ijv-gross-capacity-factor >}}.

The model accepts the wind input in two equivalent forms: a wind-state table with
a turbine curve, from which it runs PyWake itself (optional `wind` dependency), or
a stored table of per-turbine power by state. The article case stores the table,
generated with the same function by
`research_articles/turbine_level_hydrogen/analysis/prepare_common_case.py`, so
that both architectures read identical turbine power and a case run does not need
PyWake. A zero-hour design state may be added for peak-duty sizing.

## Legacy Implementation

The earlier model used a synthetic ramp-shaped power curve with a constant
thrust coefficient, PyWake's `UniformWeibullSite` with sector-edge directions, a
fixed 30° orientation and a grid truncated after $N$ positions. These are
replaced by the method above and are retained only for traceability of older
results.

::: {.callout-warning title="Remaining improvements"}
1. **Benchmark the wake model.** Compare representative dense and sparse layouts
   against at least one credible alternative wake formulation and use the
   difference as model uncertainty.
2. **Test turbulence and blockage sensitivity.** The provisional $I_0$ directly
   affects `TurboNOJDeficit`; evaluate a sourced range and quantify whether the
   omission of blockage changes the comparison.
3. **Source the minimum-separation check.** The article case keeps the unsourced
   legacy threshold of three rotor diameters as a coordinate check only.
:::

Higher-fidelity CFD, LES and full commercial layout optimisation are not proposed
at this stage. They are justified only if the simpler model has first been made
internally consistent and the remaining wake uncertainty can materially change
the comparison.
